chapters.title: How Many Kinds of Principalities There Are, and by What Means They Are Acquired
chapters.hook: A conquered gate is useless if you cannot name what kind of city stands behind it.
chapters.counterintuition: The opening mistake is to ask what a ruler should do before naming what he holds. The better move is to sort the state by form, origin, prior habit, and arms, because each label changes the danger.
chapters.tryThisNow: Take one institution in the news and label it in four columns: form of rule, old or new possession, prior habit, and basis of control. Stop before recommending any action.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Before choosing a policy, classify the possession: republic or principality, hereditary or new, free or used to rule, won by your arms, others' arms, fortune, or ability.

breakdown.fastRead: A runner lays three keys on the table after the treaty is signed. One opens a city that chose its own council. One opens a town used to a duke. One opens a valley joined to an old crown by marriage. If you call them all conquered places, you have blurred the work. Before you command, sort. Did people live free or under a prince? Is the place old, new, or joined on? Did your own force win it, or did help and luck open the gate? The first rule is not action. The first rule is naming the place well enough that action can fit it.
breakdown.deepRead:
A new ruler may want one clean order that proves the new power is in charge. That order may be tidy on paper and dangerous in the streets. The old form of rule tells you what habits people still carry. The origin of the possession tells you who feels injured or entitled. The prior habit tells you whether obedience or freedom is the memory people can rally around. The military basis tells you whether the power under you is your own, borrowed, lucky, or earned.

Picture a clerk in a captured harbor at dawn, drying rain from a stack of records. One island has a harbor charter with elected wardens. Another has a royal appointment naming a governor. A third surrendered because an allied fleet took the batteries before your ships arrived. The same flag now flies over all three. The same method will not hold all three.

Use the labels before the policy. Republics and principalities have different memories. Hereditary and new possessions have different expectations. Annexed members bring the habits of the state they came from and the claims of the state they join. Arms matter because the hand that won the gate may be the hand that can take it back.

The limit is important. Classification does not solve rule by itself. It can still be used coldly or badly. Its value is narrower and more practical: it keeps you from treating unlike dangers as one problem. A map with honest labels is not wisdom, but a map without them invites the first wrong turn.
breakdown.fullRead:
A prince who receives a province at sunrise may want the visible symbols first: guards at the gate, notices on the walls, taxes collected under the new seal. Those symbols matter less if he has not named the thing in his hand. Is it a republic or a principality? If it is a principality, is the ruling family long established, entirely new, or is the place annexed to an older state? Did the people live under a prince, or did they live in freedom? Was the acquisition made by his own arms, by the arms of others, by fortune, or by ability?

You can hear how dry those questions sound until a wrong answer causes damage. A free city may obey for a week and still remember its council hall. A hereditary town may accept a new heir if its old customs are left intact. A newly taken capital may look quiet because the soldiers are still visible. An annexed valley may seem grateful until it notices that the old ruler's taxes have been replaced by unfamiliar demands. The label is not decoration. It predicts which memory, expectation, or dependency will press back.

Picture a regent standing beside a winter road while two messengers arrive. One reports that the local nobles have sworn loyalty because their families kept their lands. The other reports that a foreign brigade has handed over the main fortress and gone home. Both reports sound like success. They are not the same success. In the first, old local power may still organize obedience or betrayal. In the second, the new ruler may be holding a fortress won by another person's strength. The next move depends on which foundation is real.

A hard objection is that rulers cannot wait forever with labels while events move. That is true. Classification is not an excuse for delay. It is the short pause that prevents a fast order from landing on the wrong surface. If the city is used to freedom, preserving a few offices may be a temporary bridge or a trap, depending on later chapters. If the state is hereditary, disturbing familiar laws may create trouble where patience would have kept peace. If the victory came through others' arms, confidence should be lower, not higher, because the force that opened the door is not fully yours.

Use the first table as a diagnostic instrument. Write down the form, origin, prior habit, and basis of acquisition. Do this before you borrow a rule from another case. A policy that works in a hereditary principality may insult a free republic. A policy that works after victory by your own arms may fail when the win came from fortune or allies. The categories are simple because the consequences are not.

The nuance is that these labels overlap. Naples can be annexed to an older crown. Milan can be entirely new to Francesco Sforza. A dominion can be used to a prince and still be new to the person who holds it now. The point is not to find one grand label and stop thinking. The point is to place several labels on the same possession so the pressure becomes visible from more than one side.

Carry one sentence into the rest of the problem: a ruler who misnames the state will misread the resistance. He may call a remembered liberty stubbornness, a borrowed army strength, a lucky opening a foundation, or an annexed member a simple province. Each mistake makes later advice sound cleaner than the situation allows.

Stand at the gate again and look past the keys. Ask what people were used to yesterday, who actually won the gate, which laws they expect tomorrow, and whether their old loyalties still have objects to gather around. Only then does the first order have a chance of matching the place it means to rule.

examples.title: Sabela Crosses Out the Single Tax Notice

planSpec.domain: a provisional governor receiving three towns after a border treaty
planSpec.audience: a civilian administrator who wants to announce one uniform policy on the first morning
planSpec.stakes: one town has elected councils, one obeyed a duke, and one was attached to the old crown by marriage, so a single decree could create three different rebellions
planSpec.requiredBeat: Before signing the tax notice, the governor pins three seals on the wall, moves the free town under republic, the ducal town under principality, and the marriage town under annexed member, then crosses out the single policy order.

examples.scenario: Three wax seals lie on a treaty map beside an unsigned tax notice at 7:10 a.m. Sabela, the provisional governor, has three town clerks waiting outside her office. One town elected its council, one obeyed a duke, and one entered the old crown through a marriage charter. Before signing, she must decide whether one order can fit them all. She pins the seals on the wall: republic, principality, annexed member. Then she crosses out the tax order.
examples.whatToDo: Keep the notice unsigned until each town has its own label. Write the first rule beside the category, not above it, so the free town, ducal town, and annexed town are not treated as one object.
examples.whyItMatters: The treaty gave Sabela possession, but it did not erase prior habits. The same tax notice would strike three different memories and create resistance she could have seen in advance.

examples.title: Adrien Sorts the Harbor Papers Before Orders

planSpec.domain: a naval prize court deciding what authority captured harbor islands had lived under
planSpec.audience: a judge advocate sorting reports before recommending occupation rules
planSpec.stakes: mislabeling elected harbor councils as former royal dependencies would send troops to solve a problem that needs preserved local law
planSpec.requiredBeat: The advocate places a harbor charter, a royal appointment, and a captain's surrender note into separate trays labeled free, princely, and won by another's arms before drafting any order.

examples.scenario: A salt-stained harbor charter curls at the edge of a prize court table near the pier at 9:05 a.m. Adrien, the judge advocate, must decide whether to send one occupation rule to the admiral. He sets three trays under a lamp. The harbor charter goes under free. A royal appointment goes under princely. A captain's surrender note from an allied frigate goes under won by another's arms. Only then does he open a blank order.
examples.whatToDo: Sort the evidence into political categories before recommending troops, councils, or courts. Let the charter, appointment, and surrender note answer what kind of authority lived there first.
examples.whyItMatters: The islands were captured together, but their authority did not come from the same source. Mislabeling a free harbor as a royal dependency would send force where law is the first issue.

examples.title: Maelle Circles the Claims Behind the Bronzes

planSpec.domain: a museum repatriation board classifying the governing claims behind disputed city bronzes
planSpec.audience: curators deciding whom to negotiate with after a regime change
planSpec.stakes: returning the bronzes to the loudest ministry could ignore a city that had governed the shrine under its own civic law
planSpec.requiredBeat: The board stops debating ownership rhetoric and circles the old civic statutes, the royal inventory stamp, and the militia seizure date in different colors to classify the claim before naming a counterparty.

examples.scenario: A bronze horse tag rests on old civic statutes in the museum boardroom at 4:20 p.m. Maelle, the curator leading the postmortem, reviews the failed call with the new ministry after everyone treated the loudest office as owner of the shrine. She must decide what rule the board carries into the next call. She circles the civic statutes in blue, the royal inventory stamp in red, and the militia seizure date in green.
examples.whatToDo: Separate the civic, royal, and seizure evidence before choosing whom to negotiate with. Treat ownership language as a prompt to classify authority, not as the classification itself.
examples.whyItMatters: The bronzes carry more than art title. A city used to its own civic law can be erased if the board treats a regime ministry, an old royal stamp, and militia force as one claim.

examples.title: Renata Turns Over the Province Evidence Cards

planSpec.domain: an election observer mission entering a province after a coup and a negotiated restoration
planSpec.audience: field observers who must decide which local actors can certify turnout
planSpec.stakes: the province may be a restored hereditary administration, a newly seized capital, or a free district coerced by soldiers, and each label changes the risk report
planSpec.requiredBeat: The team leader asks observers to predict the category, then turns over three evidence cards: family governor retained, council dissolved, garrison installed by outside troops.

examples.scenario: Laminated polling-station cards sit under a cracked evidence box in a school gym at noon. Renata, the observer lead, asks her team to predict the province category before they certify turnout actors. Then she turns over three evidence cards: family governor retained, council dissolved, outside garrison installed by foreign troops. The team must decide which local signatures can mean consent.
examples.whatToDo: Make the team classify the province before accepting signatures. Mark whether authority is hereditary, newly seized, or coerced by outside arms, then write the risk report from that label.
examples.whyItMatters: Certification is not neutral if the observers misread who holds power. A retained family governor, dissolved council, and foreign garrison point to different dangers behind the same ballot boxes.

examples.title: Benoit Marks the Valley Margins Before Rent

planSpec.domain: a monastic land steward reviewing estates after an abbot inherits and purchases neighboring valleys
planSpec.audience: a steward tempted to use the same rent roll for old abbey lands and newly acquired villages
planSpec.stakes: ancestral tenants, purchased lands, and villages used to their own councils will react differently to the same levy
planSpec.requiredBeat: Before copying last year's levy, the steward lays the abbey rent roll beside the purchase deed and the village council bell, then marks inherited, new, and accustomed to freedom in the margin.

examples.scenario: A brass council bell sits on a folded purchase deed in the abbey counting room at 5:15 a.m. Benoit, the land steward, starts to copy last year's levy onto every valley page and must decide whether old rent can cover new villages. Then he lays the abbey rent roll beside the deed and the bell. Old abbey lands get inherited. Purchased fields get new. Villages that rang their own bell get accustomed to freedom.
examples.whatToDo: Mark each estate before copying the levy. Separate inherited tenants, purchased lands, and council villages, then decide which payments can stay familiar and which need a different first approach.
examples.whyItMatters: The abbot's authority arrives through more than one path. A familiar rent on old lands may be tolerable while the same levy in a council village reads as a first injury.

examples.title: Kaoru Stops the Checkpoint Briefing at Control

planSpec.domain: a peacekeeping logistics cell mapping who actually won control of checkpoints after a ceasefire
planSpec.audience: officers deciding whether authority rests on local forces, allied troops, or accidental collapse
planSpec.stakes: a checkpoint held by local fighters can be negotiated differently from one held because a foreign brigade handed over the gate
planSpec.requiredBeat: The colonel stops the briefing at the phrase under control and makes the analyst put colored pins for own arms, others' arms, fortune, and ability on each checkpoint before approving supplies.

examples.scenario: Colored map pins are scattered beside a ceasefire checkpoint grid at 22:30. "Sector four is under control," the analyst says. Colonel Kaoru raises a hand. "Under whose control?" The foreign brigade handover log is still open. "Local fighters took blue gate," the analyst says. "Brigade handed over red. South road emptied after the flood." Kaoru must decide whether to approve supplies before the pins show own arms, others' arms, fortune, and ability.
examples.whatToDo: Stop using control as a single label. Pin each checkpoint by how it was gained, then approve supplies and negotiation channels according to local arms, outside arms, luck, or earned command.
examples.whyItMatters: A checkpoint held by local fighters is not the same as one inherited from a foreign brigade or emptied by accident. The supply plan must follow the real basis of control.

questions.prompt: At a border office, a minister receives a mountain district after a treaty. The district once elected its tax wardens, but the draft decree calls it a normal royal dependency. What should happen first?
choices: Classify the district's prior habit and form of rule before issuing the decree.
Send more collectors so the new tax order looks settled from the first week.
Ask the old royal court how it would have taxed the district before the treaty.
questions.explanation: The elected wardens point to a memory of freedom that the decree ignores. More collectors would deepen the injury, and the old court may not understand the local habit that now matters most.

questions.prompt: A harbor governor says, "We captured all five islands, so one occupation code will do." The files show two island councils, one royal governor, and two forts taken by an ally. Which reply best fits the opening sorting move?
choices: Use the same code now, then adjust after resistance appears.
Separate free councils, princely authority, and wins by others' arms before writing rules.
Focus only on which island has the largest port revenue.
questions.explanation: The files show three different political bases under one conquest. Waiting for resistance wastes the evidence already present, and revenue does not tell who is used to what form of rule.

questions.prompt: When a prince inherits his father's old province and also buys a neighboring valley whose villages kept their own assemblies, which first map is strongest?
choices: A map of roads and warehouses, because movement decides rule.
A map of the richest households, because wealth predicts loyalty.
A map marking hereditary lands, newly acquired lands, and places accustomed to freedom.
questions.explanation: The inherited province and purchased council villages will not react alike. Roads and wealth may matter later, but this first map names origin and prior habit before policy borrows the wrong rule.

questions.prompt: A commander celebrates that a fortress is now his. The report says a foreign brigade opened the gate, supplied the garrison, and plans to leave next month. What warning belongs in the first assessment?
choices: The acquisition rests on others' arms, so possession may outlast the force that made it possible.
The fortress is secure because the visible flag has changed.
The local people must be used to freedom because a foreign brigade was present.
questions.explanation: The report names the military basis: others' arms. A changed flag is only a symbol, and a foreign brigade does not by itself reveal whether the people lived freely or under a prince.

questions.prompt: In a council room, an adviser labels every new possession as a principality because each now answers to the prince. One city had been a republic until last week. What is wrong with the label?
choices: It is too respectful toward the city's old institutions.
It erases the city's prior freedom — a primary danger to classify.
It should instead classify every city by population size.
questions.explanation: Calling the city only a principality hides the republican memory that may organize resistance. Population size may affect administration, but it does not replace the first distinction about prior freedom.

questions.prompt: A restored duke returns to a province his family ruled for generations. His aide wants to replace local courts immediately to prove the restoration is real. Which response best uses the opening taxonomy?
choices: Replace the courts because inherited rule must look forceful on the first day.
Treat the province as a fresh acquisition because the brief gap in rule cancels old attachment.
Recognize the hereditary base first, then ask which familiar customs protect that attachment.
questions.explanation: The family history is part of the political fact. Immediate replacement may injure the habit that makes hereditary rule easier, while calling it entirely new throws away useful information.

questions.prompt: A regional envoy says a valley was won by ability because the new ruler is admired. The record shows a storm destroyed the rival's bridge the night before the army arrived. What should the classification note?
choices: Fortune helped open the acquisition; later ability may still be needed to hold it.
Admiration is enough to classify the win as ability.
Weather details belong in military history, not in political diagnosis.
questions.explanation: The storm is not background color. It shows fortune in the acquisition. Admiration may help later, but the first diagnosis should not pretend the opening came only from the ruler's skill.

questions.prompt: At a negotiation table, a clerk asks whether a captured town was used to freedom or used to a prince. A general says that question is academic because the town has surrendered. Why is the clerk right to ask?
choices: Because surrender by itself proves the town wanted princely rule.
Because prior habit affects what memories and institutions can organize resistance after surrender.
Because free towns rarely need garrisons once surrender papers are signed.
questions.explanation: Surrender settles the immediate fight, not the political memory. The town's old habit helps predict resistance. The other answers turn surrender into proof it cannot provide.

questions.prompt: A treaty office has four labels on the wall: republic or principality, hereditary or new, free or used to a prince, own arms or others' arms. A junior official wants to pick just one label per province. What should the supervisor say?
choices: Pick the easiest label so the order can be written quickly.
Use only the military label because arms decide everything else.
Keep multiple labels when they apply, because each one names a different pressure.
questions.explanation: A province can be annexed, used to a prince, and won by allies at the same time. Choosing one neat label hides pressures that may matter in different parts of the first order.

reviewCards.front: A city has surrendered, but its council hall still holds elected records. What is the first question?
reviewCards.back: Ask whether the people were accustomed to freedom before treating surrender as settled obedience. The old form of rule tells you what memory may still gather resistance.

reviewCards.front: A fortress was handed over by an allied army. Which label should slow your confidence?
reviewCards.back: Won by others' arms. The gate may be yours, but the force that opened it is not fully yours, so the foundation is weaker than it looks.

reviewCards.front: A ruler inherits one town and annexes another. Why not give both the same first order?
reviewCards.back: Hereditary and annexed possessions carry different expectations. The inherited town may value continuity, while the annexed town may still compare every order with its prior state.

reviewCards.front: A report says the province is new, used to princely rule, and gained by fortune. Can all three labels matter?
reviewCards.back: Yes. The labels answer different questions: origin, prior habit, and basis of acquisition. Keeping all three visible prevents a clean but false diagnosis.

reviewCards.front: Before recommending a policy for a newly held place, what four columns should you fill?
reviewCards.back: Form of rule, old or new status, prior habit of the people, and basis of control. Action comes after the possession has been named from those angles.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice classifying power before prescribing action. In any political or institutional case, name the form, origin, prior habit, and basis of control before you argue for a policy.

ifThenPlans.context: Reading a news story about a takeover
ifThenPlans.plan: If a report says a leader now controls a city, then write how the city was governed before the takeover and how control was gained before judging the next move.
If someone says the new authority has won, then ask whether the win rests on its own arms, someone else's arms, fortune, or ability.
If two places look administratively similar, then check whether one is hereditary, new, annexed, or accustomed to freedom before borrowing the same rule.
If you feel ready to recommend a policy, then pause and fill the four labels first: form, origin, prior habit, and basis of control.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Choose one current conflict, merger of authorities, or disputed territory in the news. In four short lines, label form of rule, old or new status, prior habit, and basis of control, then write one sentence you would not have written before labeling.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once this week, take a political story that tempts you into quick judgment and build a four-column classification table before reading opinion about it.

memorableLines.text: The first rule is not action.
memorableLines.why: It turns the opening taxonomy into a concrete restraint on premature policy.

memorableLines.text: A map with honest labels is not wisdom, but a map without them invites the first wrong turn.
memorableLines.why: It states both the value and the limit of classification in one usable image.

memorableLines.text: a ruler who misnames the state will misread the resistance.
memorableLines.why: It connects the naming act to the practical danger the chapter is built to prevent.

chapters.title: Concerning Hereditary Principalities
chapters.hook: The old ferry bell buys patience until the new captain moves the first boat.
chapters.counterintuition: Inherited rule is not safe because people adore old names. It is safer because old motives for change have faded, unless the new holder creates fresh injuries by disturbing customs that made the house bearable.
chapters.tryThisNow: Name one role that survives because people are used to it. Make two columns: customs not to disturb first, and circumstances that may need quiet adaptation.
chapters.keyTakeaway: A hereditary state stays easier to hold when the new ruler preserves familiar customs, avoids needless offense, and adapts only where circumstances truly require it.

breakdown.fastRead: A new captain takes the ferry keys while islanders stamp snow from their boots. Her family has run the route for decades, so passengers are already well disposed. That patience is an asset, not a blank check. If she moves the first boat, changes the dock ritual, and rewrites crew turns in one week, she invites resentment. People had accepted her house before. Hereditary rule is held by preserving familiar customs first, then adapting only where circumstances make change necessary.
breakdown.deepRead:
Nobody needs to persuade the islanders that the captain's family belongs on the route. The old attachment is already there. That is why inherited power can be easier to hold than new power. The subjects have lived with the family. The sharp memories of past change have worn down. Ordinary government can continue without proving itself every morning.

The danger begins when the heir mistakes that ease for permission. People may forgive weather, scarcity, and the normal trouble of life under a familiar ruler. They are less forgiving when the familiar ruler creates a needless new offense. A toll collected in the old way may pass with grumbling. A surprise fee under the new seal may feel like insult. A procession that has moved through the same gate for generations can carry more consent than the custodian realizes.

Picture Ferrara's duke facing stronger enemies. His rule had lasted long enough that subjects held a settled attachment before extraordinary force arrived. The lesson is not that old rule is invincible. A usurper can still seize it. The point is that when the usurper stumbles, a familiar house may return because people have fewer living motives for change.

Use the inherited attachment carefully. Keep the customs that make rule feel continuous. Handle new conditions as they arise. The limit is clear: custom is not sacred just because it is old. If drought, war, debt, or safety requires change, adapt. But attach the change to the old order where you can, so people see necessity rather than contempt.
breakdown.fullRead:
The red timetable stamp is clean, the old manifest is stiff with frost, and the deckhands already know the 6:10 loading order by memory. Eirlys could prove command by changing the whole morning. She could also spend the trust her family took decades to gather.

Hereditary rule begins with an advantage that new rule lacks. People are used to the family of the prince. Old shocks have softened. The daily habits of obedience, petition, toll, route, festival, court, or water turn are already attached to a name. That does not make subjects innocent or rulers beloved in a warm sense. It means fewer fresh motives exist for a change. A prince of average powers can often remain in place if he does not transgress the customs of his ancestors and if he handles new circumstances with prudence.

A temple keeper with an iron festival key learns the same thing. The procession gate is crowded, and moving it would make crowd control easier. Yet the chalk marks on the threshold show where families have stood for years. If he repairs the rope and keeps the gate, the town sees care. If he moves the procession on his first festival, the same crowd problem becomes a sign that the new keeper holds the old route in contempt. The practical difference is not tradition versus reform. The difference is whether change begins by injuring the custom that made consent available.

A fair objection is that old customs can be inefficient, unjust, or too weak for new pressure. The source does not ask the ruler to freeze. It says to deal prudently with circumstances as they arise. A watermaster facing a dry summer may have to change the ditch schedule. A coroner may need a better database. A toll warden may need repairs after a usurper briefly holds the gate. The mistake is not adaptation. The mistake is treating adaptation as a chance to show that the new holder is finally free from the inherited pattern.

The Duke of Ferrara shows the outer edge. Long duration in his dominions helped him withstand attacks that might have broken a newer ruler. That advantage did not come from magic blood or noble romance. It came from time, habit, and the lack of fresh offense. When rule has lasted, people often lose the clear memory and motive that make change feel worth the risk. If extraordinary and excessive force removes such a ruler, the usurper must then avoid becoming the new offense. When anything sinister happens to the usurper, the old line has a path back.

Do not confuse this with comfort. Hereditary rule is still political work. The heir must ask which customs carry attachment and which details can move without insult. The first list deserves protection. The second list may be changed slowly, with reasons tied to a visible circumstance. If the ferry route faces ice, move the boat because ice demands it, not because the new captain wants a cleaner stamp. If the festival gate is unsafe, strengthen the rope, widen the steward line, or explain the one necessary change through the old keepers before replacing the route.

The deeper rule is spare: do not manufacture reasons for people to hate what they had learned to tolerate. Subjects who are well disposed by duration can become hostile when a familiar hand starts acting like a conqueror. Old attachment is a store of patience. Spend it only on necessity, never on vanity.

Carry that into any inherited office. Before the new notice, new fee, new schedule, or new procession route, ask what the old practice was doing besides being old. It may have made grief bearable, order visible, rank predictable, or scarcity feel shared. Preserve that function first. Then adapt with care.

examples.title: Eirlys Sets Down the Red Timetable Stamp

planSpec.domain: a long-established ferry charter on a winter island route after the captain's daughter inherits command
planSpec.audience: an heir who wants to modernize the route announcement, ticket booth hours, and crew rotations in her first week
planSpec.stakes: islanders tolerate weather delays because the family has served the route for decades, but changing the first boat and dock ritual could turn patience into resentment
planSpec.requiredBeat: She reaches for the new timetable stamp, hears the deckhands call the old 6:10 loading order by memory, and puts the stamp down until she has marked which customs actually hold the route together.

examples.scenario: A red timetable stamp sits beside a frost-stiff ferry manifest at 5:48 a.m. Eirlys, the new captain on the winter island route, reaches for it to mark the first revised schedule of her command. Outside, deckhands call the old 6:10 loading order by memory while passengers line up without looking at the board. She must decide whether her first week should move the route or first mark which customs hold the route together.
examples.whatToDo: Put the stamp down and list the customs that create patience: the 6:10 loading order, booth hours, and crew turns. Change only what weather, safety, or debt truly requires.
examples.whyItMatters: The islanders already accept her family at the helm. A new schedule may be useful later, but a needless first change would turn inherited patience into fresh resentment.

examples.title: Samir Keeps the Procession Gate

planSpec.domain: a hereditary temple custodianship where a new keeper takes over festival keys
planSpec.audience: a young custodian tempted to move the festival procession for crowd control
planSpec.stakes: the town accepts the family key because the procession route has survived generations, and a small route change could look like contempt
planSpec.requiredBeat: With the festival key in his hand, the keeper traces the old chalk marks on the stone threshold and chooses to repair the crowd rope instead of moving the procession gate.

examples.scenario: An iron festival key rests in Samir's palm on the temple threshold at 6:30 p.m. White chalk marks from last year's procession still cross the stone. The crowd rope is frayed near the east gate, and a constable suggests moving the procession to the wider lane. Samir traces the old marks with his thumb and must decide whether his first festival should move the gate or repair the rope.
examples.whatToDo: Repair the crowd rope and keep the procession gate for the first festival. If safety later requires a change, explain it through the old route and the families who know it.
examples.whyItMatters: The town accepts Samir's key because the route feels continuous. Moving the gate first would make crowd control look like contempt for the custom that carries consent.

examples.title: Ioana Clips the Old Tokens to the Drought Chart

planSpec.domain: a mountain irrigation district whose watermaster role has passed through one household for a century
planSpec.audience: a successor reading snowpack data and old ditch schedules before the first dry summer meeting
planSpec.stakes: farmers will forgive a dry year more readily than a new watermaster who silently changes ancestral turn order
planSpec.requiredBeat: Before presenting the drought chart, she clips the old wooden turn tokens to the new snowpack board so everyone sees adaptation attached to inherited order.

examples.scenario: Wooden water-turn tokens hang from a nail above a snowpack chart in the district shed at 7:15 a.m. Before the dry summer meeting, Ioana studies the old ditch schedule her grandmother used and the new numbers that show half the meltwater. She is about to present only the drought chart. Instead, she clips the old tokens to the snowpack board so the farmers see adaptation attached to inherited order.
examples.whatToDo: Present the dry-year change beside the old tokens and ditch schedule. Show which turns must shift because of water, and which inherited order remains untouched.
examples.whyItMatters: Farmers may endure scarcity more readily than silent disrespect. The tokens show that Ioana is adapting to drought, not using drought to erase the order they know.

examples.title: Cormac Reopens His Uncle's Call Ledger

planSpec.domain: a county coroner's office after a respected elected coroner's nephew wins the seat
planSpec.audience: a new official who inherits public trust but also inherited burial notification customs
planSpec.stakes: families accept grim news partly because the office's old procedure feels stable, and a rushed software-only notice could create hatred from a needless offense
planSpec.requiredBeat: After the first complaint, the nephew places the unopened digital notice beside his uncle's worn call ledger and restores the personal call before changing the database workflow.

examples.scenario: A worn call ledger lies open beside an unopened digital notice on Cormac's desk at 8:40 p.m. The first complaint since he won his uncle's coroner seat is clipped to a family notification card. Cormac had let the database send the message before anyone called. In the postmortem, he places the digital notice beside the ledger and must decide what procedure returns before the workflow changes again.
examples.whatToDo: Restore the personal call before changing the database workflow. Keep the notification card and ledger sequence visible while the software is made to support, not replace, the old practice.
examples.whyItMatters: The office inherited trust in a cruel moment. A software-only notice creates a needless offense where the old call custom made grim authority bearable.

examples.title: Laleh Places the Paddle Across the Queue Form

planSpec.domain: a tribal canoe-fishing permit held by one chiefly line under a regional compact
planSpec.audience: a new permit holder negotiating with fisheries officers and village elders
planSpec.stakes: state inspectors may focus on quotas, but village consent depends on keeping the inherited landing sequence visible
planSpec.requiredBeat: When the officer asks for a new numbered queue, the permit holder lays the carved landing paddle across the form and asks which rule can change without touching the ancestral order.

examples.scenario: A carved landing paddle covers the corner of a permit-renewal form at the fisheries office at 11:05 a.m. "Number the canoes by arrival," the officer says. Laleh must decide whether to accept the new queue before the elders speak. "The quota page can change," she says, placing the paddle across the form. "Which rule can change without touching the landing sequence?" The officer taps his pen and waits.
examples.whatToDo: Separate the quota rule from the inherited landing order. Negotiate the numbered record around the sequence elders recognize, instead of making consent depend on a new queue.
examples.whyItMatters: Inspectors need a count, but village consent rests on the visible order of landing. Laleh protects the custom while making room for the compact's record.

examples.title: Nestor Rehangs the Copper Toll Scale

planSpec.domain: a centuries-old market toll gate where a new hereditary warden faces a rival's attempted seizure
planSpec.audience: a warden trying to keep merchants loyal after an outside usurper briefly controlled the gate
planSpec.stakes: the rival's force may fade, but merchants will return only if the familiar toll practice resumes without punitive surprise fees
planSpec.requiredBeat: The warden predicts loyalty will return when the usurper stumbles, then proves it by rehanging the old copper toll scale and refusing to add a recovery surcharge.

examples.scenario: A copper toll scale swings from an empty market arch at 4:55 a.m. Nestor, the new hereditary warden, reads the rival's notice still pasted to the post and predicts the merchants will return now that the usurper's guards have fled. His clerk points to a recovery surcharge line. Nestor rehanges the old scale, strikes out the surcharge, and must decide whether familiar practice is stronger than revenge.
examples.whatToDo: Resume the old toll practice before seeking repayment. Rehang the copper scale, remove the recovery surcharge, and let merchants see that the usurper's seizure did not create a new injury.
examples.whyItMatters: The rival's force may fade on its own. Merchants return when the old gate feels familiar again, not when the restored warden punishes them for surviving the seizure.

questions.prompt: When a new hereditary toll keeper inherits a gate that merchants have used for decades, and he wants to add a welcome fee on the first market day to pay for repairs, what is the best first move?
choices: Keep the familiar toll practice at first and find repairs that do not create a surprise injury.
Add the fee immediately so merchants learn the new keeper has authority.
Close the gate for a week so the merchants appreciate the old arrangement.
questions.explanation: The old toll already carries some acceptance. A surprise fee creates a fresh motive for resentment, while closing the gate manufactures the same kind of needless offense.

questions.prompt: The canal office has passed through one household for generations. A dry season forces rationing. Which response best separates prudent adaptation from transgressing custom?
choices: Replace the whole turn order because drought proves the old system is obsolete.
Show the shortage beside the old turn order; change only turns the water level requires.
Refuse adaptation because inherited customs in this canal office should be preserved unchanged.
questions.explanation: The shortage is a real circumstance, so some change may be needed. Keeping the old order visible shows necessity. Replacing everything or freezing everything both miss prudence.

questions.prompt: The festival custodian inherits a route accepted for generations. The east rope is unsafe, but the route itself still works. What should he do first?
choices: Move the whole procession to prove he takes safety seriously.
Cancel the procession and blame the old route.
Repair the rope and preserve the gate unless safety truly requires more.
questions.explanation: The unsafe rope is the circumstance that needs action, not proof that the whole custom should be disturbed. Moving the route first makes repair look like contempt.

questions.prompt: After a restored hereditary ruler returns following an extraordinary force that removed him for six months, the usurper has become hated. Why might subjects accept the old ruler again?
choices: Duration left fewer old motives for change, and the usurper created new ones.
Subjects in a hereditary state default to any ruler bearing the old family name.
A brief removal proves the old ruler no longer needs to respect local customs.
questions.explanation: The return works because old attachment can survive removal when the usurper becomes the fresh offense. Name alone is not enough, and ignoring customs would squander the advantage.

questions.prompt: A new coroner inherits public trust from a respected uncle. He sends automated death notices before any personal call, then receives angry complaints. What did he misread?
choices: He thought technology was inherently faster, so the notices should have used more formal language.
He relied on inherited trust while disturbing the notification custom that made the office bearable.
He should have hidden the change until families got used to it.
questions.explanation: The inherited office had trust partly because its old call procedure softened grim authority. Better wording or secrecy does not fix the fresh offense of replacing the first human contact.

questions.prompt: A new heir says, "People are used to my family, so I can redesign the court schedule, market fees, and petition day this month." Which correction is strongest?
choices: He should redesign only the court schedule because courts matter less than fees.
He should wait until people forget every old custom.
Familiarity lowers friction only if he avoids creating new injuries to customs people count on.
questions.explanation: The heir treats duration as a blank check. The safer rule is to protect the familiar practices first. Picking one change at random still misses which customs carry consent.

questions.prompt: A fisheries officer wants a numbered queue for canoes, but village consent depends on an inherited landing sequence. Which plan best fits hereditary prudence?
choices: Keep the landing sequence visible while adding a record that satisfies the quota rule.
Adopt the numbered queue because state paperwork is more current.
Reject all paperwork because inherited practice settles every question.
questions.explanation: The quota record can adapt around the landing sequence. The numbered queue would disturb the visible custom, while rejecting all paperwork ignores a circumstance that must be handled.

questions.prompt: A hereditary ferry captain wants to modernize announcements, booth hours, and crew rotations in her first week. Passengers already trust the family route. What should she ask first?
choices: Which changes will prove she is not just copying her ancestors?
Which customs actually hold passenger patience together, and which circumstances require quiet change?
Which passenger complaints can be ignored because the family has held the charter for decades?
questions.explanation: The useful split is between customs that carry attachment and circumstances that truly require adaptation. Proving independence or ignoring complaints both misuse inherited patience.

questions.prompt: A rival briefly seizes an old market gate and flees. The restored warden wants a recovery surcharge from merchants who traded during the seizure. What is the main risk?
choices: The surcharge may turn restoration into a fresh offense and make the familiar gate feel punitive.
The merchants will assume the rival was rightful unless they are fined.
The old toll scale will matter less than a public victory speech.
questions.explanation: The warden's advantage is the return of a familiar practice after the usurper stumbles. A surcharge creates a new injury, while fines and speeches distract from restoring the old toll.

reviewCards.front: A new heir enters a settled office. What should she protect before making visible changes?
reviewCards.back: Protect the customs that make people already willing to accept the office. Hereditary advantage works through familiar practice, not through permission to offend.

reviewCards.front: A dry summer forces a hereditary watermaster to change turns. What makes the change prudent?
reviewCards.back: Tie the change to the visible circumstance and keep the inherited order present where possible. Prudence adapts to need without making the old custom look despised.

reviewCards.front: An usurper removes a long-established ruler, then becomes hated. Why can the old ruler return?
reviewCards.back: Duration may have left subjects with fewer motives for change, while the usurper creates fresh ones. The old line returns through familiar attachment, not magic legitimacy.

reviewCards.front: A familiar toll gate adds a surprise fee after restoration. What mistake is being made?
reviewCards.back: The warden is turning inherited attachment into a new injury. The safer move is to resume the familiar toll first and spend trust only on necessities.

reviewCards.front: What two lists should a new hereditary holder make before reforming anything?
reviewCards.back: List customs that carry acceptance and circumstances that require adaptation. Change belongs in the second list and should disturb the first as little as possible.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: When you inherit a role, office, route, or procedure, find the customs that already create acceptance. Preserve those first, then adapt only where a visible circumstance makes change necessary.

ifThenPlans.context: Taking over a familiar public role
ifThenPlans.plan: If people already trust the role because it feels familiar, then list the customs they count on before changing hours, fees, routes, or first contacts.
If drought, safety, debt, or staffing forces change, then attach the change to the visible pressure and preserve the old order wherever it still works.

ifThenPlans.context: Restoring authority after a rival or predecessor caused disruption
ifThenPlans.plan: If you return after someone else disturbed the office, then resume the familiar practice before adding penalties, surcharges, or proofs of strength.
If your main reason for change is to show you are different from your ancestors, then pause and ask what new motive for resentment the change would create.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Find one inherited procedure in your workplace, town, school, or family office. Write two columns: what familiar custom creates acceptance, and what current circumstance might justify a careful change.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once this week, watch a new holder of an old role. Before judging them, note whether they preserve the custom that carries trust or disturb it to prove command.

memorableLines.text: That patience is an asset, not a blank check.
memorableLines.why: It separates inherited attachment from permission to disrupt.

memorableLines.text: custom is not sacred just because it is old.
memorableLines.why: It keeps the chapter from becoming nostalgia while preserving the source's warning about needless offense.

memorableLines.text: Old attachment is a store of patience.
memorableLines.why: It gives the central mechanism a compact image the reader can carry into examples.

chapters.title: Concerning Mixed Principalities
chapters.hook: The port gates open at dawn, and the men who helped you enter are already angry by noon.
chapters.counterintuition: Annexation closes nothing. In fact, the flag changing marks the start: injuries, disorders, jealous neighbors, and minor powers must be governed at close range instead of celebrated as victory.
chapters.tryThisNow: Pick one recent takeover or occupation in public affairs. Write four pressures: injured locals, disappointed helpers, rules too dangerous to touch, and the outside power malcontents could invite.
chapters.keyTakeaway: A mixed principality is stabilized by reducing new injuries, staying near early trouble, using small local anchors, guarding minor powers, and blocking foreign entrants.

breakdown.fastRead: The port gates open at dawn, and the dockworkers who helped the new authority enter carry a petition by noon. They expected relief. Warehouse owners fear seizure. Capital officials will hear about a riot only after it has a banner. Victory is the start of the transition, not the end of the problem. In a mixed principality, the ruler must limit new injuries and stay close enough to see trouble early. Leave laws and taxes alone when possible. Block any foreign power that angry locals might invite in.
breakdown.deepRead:
Dockworkers who open a gate may become angry before the new flag is dry. The people injured by seizure resent the burdens of soldiers, taxes, officials, and broken hopes. The people who helped open the gates feel deceived when they do not receive the reward they imagined. The new ruler cannot crush those helpers easily because he still depends on local goodwill. That is why a mixed principality is not secured the moment a new ruler walks in.

Picture an administrator in a port customs house with a bilingual tax ledger under her hand. If she governs from the capital, she will hear of disorders only when they are already large. A distant ruler hears about disorders only after they have become organized. If she resides there, she sees the first three angry men at the counter and can answer before a faction forms.

Watch a garrison ride the same rail line every day, and the lesson changes shape. A garrison marches hardship through the whole territory and makes many people hostile. A small colony injures fewer people, though the injury is still real, and gives the ruler a local anchor at lower cost. The rule is not kindness for its own sake. It is the arithmetic of resentment.

Keep one limit in view. Avoiding every hard act can lose the state, but scattering pain everywhere is worse. Keep the old laws and taxes when similarity makes union easy. When speech, habits, or laws differ, stay near the trouble and injure fewer people. Protect minor powers without enlarging them. Never let a stronger outsider become the shelter for malcontents.
breakdown.fullRead:
A mixed principality is hard because it is neither fully new nor comfortably old. It is an added member, joined to an older state, and the join is where trouble starts. Men may welcome a new ruler because they hope to better themselves. Then they discover soldiers in their streets, unfamiliar officials at their counters, or taxes that do not match the promise. Hope becomes resentment. The new ruler has injured locals in taking the place and disappointed friends who expected more from helping him enter.

In Milan, Louis XII took the city quickly and lost it quickly. The first loss was not mysterious. Those who had opened the gates found that the new prince did not give the future benefit they expected. Lodovico could stir the borders because disappointment had already done part of the work. A second conquest can be harder to lose because rebellion gives the ruler excuse to punish, clear suspects, and strengthen weak places. But that does not erase the first lesson: entry is not possession if the transition creates enemies faster than it creates order.

You can hold an annexed place more easily when it shares country, language, customs, and prior obedience. Then the ruler can often preserve old conditions, avoid altering laws and taxes, and remove the former ruling family. The danger grows when language, customs, or laws differ. Then good fortune and energy are not enough from a distance. The ruler should reside there, because he sees disorders as they spring up and officials cannot pillage unchecked behind his back. Subjects who want to be good have quicker recourse. Those who mean harm know the ruler is present.

A fair objection is that residence is costly and colonies are harsh. Both can be true. The comparison is not between harm and purity. It is between limited, visible anchoring and a roving garrison that turns the whole state into a bill for occupation. A garrison consumes revenue, spreads hardship, and lets every village meet the new rule as a burden. Colonies injure fewer people than garrisons, but the injured still count. If you use them, you are choosing a narrow injury to prevent a wider one. That choice should not be romanticized.

Regional balance matters as much as local pain. The new ruler should become the head and defender of minor powers while preventing them from growing strong enough to challenge him. He should weaken greater powers and keep out any foreign power as strong as himself. Discontented people will invite such an outsider through ambition or fear. Once a strong foreigner gains a footing, every subject state that hates the current ruler has a place to rally.

After Lombardy, the French king did the opposite in Italy. He strengthened the Church by helping Pope Alexander take Romagna. He brought Spain into the kingdom of Naples. He did not settle in the country. He did not send colonies. He weakened minor powers and then mishandled the Venetians, who had helped him enter Lombardy. The pattern is plain: he traded a difficult transition for a regional structure that made France less necessary and gave the discontented stronger places to shelter.

The hardest warning is about deferred war. A ruler may divide a problem with Spain, admit a stronger ally, or put off a fight with a powerful neighbor and call that prudence. Do not commit a blunder to avoid a war that delay will hand to someone else. War is not always avoidable. Sometimes it is only postponed to another power's advantage. The prudent move is to see future trouble while it is still small enough to treat.

Carry the rule into any annexation. Ask who was hurt by entry, who helped and now expects too much, which laws and taxes must not be touched yet, where the ruler must be physically present, whether a local colony or a roaming force spreads less resentment, which minor powers need protection, and which outside power must be kept from the door. The map is not secure because your color is on it. It is secure only when the pressures under that color have been managed before they mature.

examples.title: Zuleika Moves Into the Port Customs House

planSpec.domain: a postwar civilian authority annexing a port district with a different language and tax code
planSpec.audience: an administrator deciding between governing from the capital or moving into the port
planSpec.stakes: dockworkers who opened the gates expect relief, warehouse owners fear confiscation, and distant officials will hear of riots only after they are organized
planSpec.requiredBeat: She folds the capital-office lease, pins a desk tag inside the port customs house, and watches the first tax protest form while it is still three men at a counter.

examples.scenario: A customs-house desk tag lies beside a bilingual tax ledger at 8:25 a.m. Zuleika, the civilian administrator, has a capital-office lease in one folder and a dockworkers' petition in another. Three warehouse men are already arguing at the counter over the new tax code. She folds the lease, pins her desk tag inside the port customs house, and must decide to watch the protest while it is still three men rather than a riot.
examples.whatToDo: Reside in the port long enough to see disorders early. Keep the tax ledger open, answer the dockworkers' petition in person, and delay rule changes that are not needed this week.
examples.whyItMatters: The port differs in language and tax habit. A capital office would hear about anger after it organizes, while presence lets Zuleika limit injury before factions form.

examples.title: Ciro Moves the Station Keys Off the Requisition

planSpec.domain: a rail authority absorbing an independent mountain line after its board invited help
planSpec.audience: a transport commissioner tempted to fill every station with armed fare inspectors
planSpec.stakes: the old board expected investment, riders expected lower fares, and a roaming enforcement force would make every village feel conquered
planSpec.requiredBeat: The commissioner moves six brass station keys from the garrison request onto two permanent depot posts, showing the choice to plant small local presence instead of sending inspectors up and down the line.

examples.scenario: Six brass station keys sit on top of an enforcement requisition in the mountain rail office at 10:10 p.m. Ciro, the transport commissioner, studies a fare chart the old board said would fall after annexation. His staff wants armed inspectors riding every train by Monday. Ciro must decide whether to spread hardship along the line or plant a smaller presence. He moves the keys from the garrison request onto two permanent depot posts.
examples.whatToDo: Use two permanent depot posts before roaming armed inspectors. Keep fares stable for the first week, answer the old board's investment promise, and avoid making every village meet the takeover as force.
examples.whyItMatters: A moving garrison would teach the whole line to feel conquered. Small local anchors injure fewer people and give the authority a place to hear trouble early.

examples.title: Thandi Turns the Patrol Nameplates Face Down

planSpec.domain: a river-delta protectorate managing minor chiefs after a neighboring empire offers them troops
planSpec.audience: a resident envoy balancing local allies against a stronger outside power
planSpec.stakes: weak chiefs can help hold the delta only if they are protected without being enlarged enough to challenge the protectorate
planSpec.requiredBeat: The envoy asks which chief should receive the seized patrol boats, then turns the boats' nameplates face down and instead assigns escort schedules that protect each chief without adding territory.

examples.scenario: Patrol-boat nameplates are stacked beside a river-delta chart at the envoy's table at 3:20 p.m. Thandi, the resident envoy, reads a foreign troop offer from the neighboring empire and must decide whether one minor chief should receive the seized boats. Her aides predict Chief Ora, who controls the north creek. Thandi turns the nameplates face down and assigns escort schedules instead, protecting each chief without adding territory.
examples.whatToDo: Decline the foreign troop offer and avoid giving patrol boats to one chief. Protect the minor powers with escort schedules while keeping any single ally from becoming large enough to threaten the delta.
examples.whyItMatters: Weak chiefs are useful only if they stay weak and protected. Enlarging one creates a future rival, while foreign troops would give every malcontent a stronger patron.

examples.title: Paloma Stamps the Medicine Order First

planSpec.domain: a provincial health ministry taking over a border hospital network that kept its own hiring rules
planSpec.audience: a minister deciding whether to replace local rules immediately after acquisition
planSpec.stakes: patients want better supplies, nurses fear lost seniority, and altering pay tables before trust forms could turn a welcomed takeover into a hostile one
planSpec.requiredBeat: Before issuing the standard pay grid, the minister sets the old seniority cards beside the provincial salary sheet and stamps only the medicine-supply order for the first week.

examples.scenario: Old seniority cards fan out beside a provincial salary sheet in Paloma's ministry car at 6:50 a.m. Before the border hospitals open under provincial control, she prepares a standard pay grid. Then the head nurse's note arrives: patients want medicine, nurses fear lost seniority. Paloma sets the cards beside the salary sheet and stamps only the medicine-supply order for the first week.
examples.whatToDo: Send medicine first and leave the seniority rules untouched while trust forms. Study the old hiring rules before replacing pay tables that nurses read as protection.
examples.whyItMatters: The takeover was welcomed for supplies, not for immediate injury to rank. Touching pay and seniority too soon would turn helpers and patients into separate sources of resistance.

examples.title: Idris Marks Both Oasis Demands as Injuries

planSpec.domain: a desert oasis district added to an old kingdom after local merchants funded the campaign
planSpec.audience: a tax governor trying to satisfy merchants who helped him enter the district
planSpec.stakes: the merchants want monopoly privileges, farmers fear new levies, and the governor cannot crush allies he still depends on
planSpec.requiredBeat: When the merchants slide a monopoly charter across the date table, the governor places it beside the farmers' water-tax tablets and marks both as injuries that would create enemies if granted whole.

examples.scenario: A folded monopoly charter rests beside clay water-tax tablets at the date-market gate. "We funded your entry," the lead merchant says, sliding the charter to Idris. "And we fed your horses," a farmer says, tapping the tablets. Idris must decide whether to please one ally by injuring the other. He places the charter beside the water-tax tablets and writes injury on both margins. "Granted whole, either one makes enemies."
examples.whatToDo: Refuse to pay helpers with a full monopoly or farmers with a sudden levy. Name both demands as injuries, then offer narrow relief that does not create a larger hostile group.
examples.whyItMatters: The merchants helped open the district, but satisfying them whole would injure farmers. The new governor must limit disappointment without turning allies' rewards into local hatred.

examples.title: Vesna Rewrites Avoided War as Deferred War

planSpec.domain: a league of city-states deciding whether to invite a distant kingdom to counter a rival after annexing a valley
planSpec.audience: councillors tempted to divide the valley question with a powerful outsider to avoid immediate war
planSpec.stakes: sharing control may postpone fighting but gives every malcontent a stronger patron and may make the outsider master of the whole region
planSpec.requiredBeat: The clerk draws arrows from the valley rebels to the distant king's seal, then writes deferred war on the margin where the council had written avoided war.

examples.scenario: A distant king's seal is pressed into the corner of a valley map in the league archive at 3:30 p.m. Vesna, the council clerk, reconstructs why the valley rebels now ignore league summons. Last spring the council wrote avoided war beside the invitation to the kingdom. Vesna draws arrows from the rebels to the king's seal, then writes deferred war in the margin where the old minutes had celebrated peace.
examples.whatToDo: Treat the invitation as a new danger, not a settled peace. Trace which malcontents now have a stronger patron and plan to block the outsider's authority before it becomes regional mastery.
examples.whyItMatters: The council postponed a fight by admitting a foreign power. That gave rebels a shelter and changed the balance from a valley dispute into a threat to the whole league.

questions.prompt: After the capital annexes a port where dockworkers opened the gates, by the second day the dockworkers demand jobs and warehouse owners fear confiscation. What is the first pressure map?
choices: List injured locals, disappointed helpers, touched rules, and any outsider they might invite.
Celebrate the dockworkers as loyal and ignore the warehouse owners until they protest.
Move all decisions to the capital so local anger cannot pressure the new authority.
questions.explanation: The port already has both early enemy groups: injured locals and helpers expecting reward. Governing from afar or favoring one group lets resentment organize before anyone sees it.

questions.prompt: When a new ruler holds a district with a different language and tax code, his officials say reports from the capital are enough. Which answer best follows the mixed-principality rule?
choices: Trust reports because distance keeps the ruler above local quarrels.
Reside there or keep a close local seat so small disorders are seen early.
Change the tax code immediately so everyone knows which law governs.
questions.explanation: Difference in language and tax habit makes early trouble easy to miss. Residence lets the ruler answer small disorders. Distance and instant tax changes both increase the risk.

questions.prompt: The annexed rail line has villages along every station. The commissioner can send armed inspectors through the whole line or create two permanent depot posts. Why choose the posts first?
choices: Because permanent posts along the rail line guarantee no station villager is injured.
Because armed inspectors are barred by treaty in this annexed rail line.
Because a roaming force spreads hardship across stations, while small anchors create presence with fewer injuries.
questions.explanation: The choice is not harmless versus harmful. It is narrower injury and local presence versus a moving burden that teaches every station to feel occupied.

questions.prompt: Suppose the border hospital network welcomes a provincial takeover for medicine, and the minister also wants to replace seniority rules in week one. What is the strongest warning?
choices: Send the medicine first and avoid turning a welcomed supply fix into an injury to rank.
Replace the seniority rules first because gratitude for medicine will cover the change.
Delay medicine until the nurses accept the provincial pay grid.
questions.explanation: The welcome is tied to supplies, not to every rule change. Touching seniority before trust forms creates a needless injury among the people needed to run the hospitals.

questions.prompt: A protectorate has three weak chiefs and one larger neighbor offering troops. One adviser wants to give seized patrol boats to the most loyal chief. What is the risk?
choices: The loyal chief will, by being shielded, become less useful to the protectorate over time.
Enlarging one minor power may create a rival; foreign troops can shelter malcontents in the protectorate.
All minor powers should be crushed immediately because protectorate allies tend to grow rivalrous.
questions.explanation: Minor powers should be protected without being enlarged. The patrol boats change one ally's weight, while foreign troops give the resentful a stronger outside patron.

questions.prompt: A ruler can divide a disputed valley with a distant kingdom to avoid war this year. The valley rebels already admire that kingdom. What judgment best fits the warning about delay?
choices: Any delay is good because time usually dissolves political tension.
Sharing the valley may be harmless if both sides sign a careful treaty.
The deal may only defer war while giving rebels a stronger patron.
questions.explanation: The issue is not treaty neatness. Inviting a strong foreign power gives malcontents somewhere to rally and can postpone conflict to the outsider's advantage.

questions.prompt: A province shares language and customs with the old kingdom that annexed it. The old ruling family is gone. Which first restraint matters most?
choices: Preserve laws and taxes where possible so union can feel continuous.
Install a garrison in every town to prevent nostalgia.
Invite a foreign arbiter to reassure local nobles.
questions.explanation: Similarity makes union easier if ordinary conditions are left alone. Garrisoning spreads hardship, and a foreign arbiter creates the outside foothold the ruler should avoid.

questions.prompt: A city league annexes a valley, then strengthens a powerful neighboring church to keep another rival quiet. What has the league done wrong?
choices: It should have ignored every small ally and backed only the strongest force.
It has strengthened a greater power in the region, making its own hold less secure.
It has spent too much time on future trouble and not enough on current peace.
questions.explanation: The regional balance matters. Strengthening a greater power repeats the error of making another actor less dependent and more able to shelter discontent.

questions.prompt: A governor says, "The people who opened the gates are our friends, so we can satisfy them later." What answer best names the danger?
choices: Gate-openers stop being useful once conquest of the city is complete.
Friends should receive every reward they ask for, even if locals are injured.
Helpers become enemies when expected benefits fail, but paying them too fully can injure other locals.
questions.explanation: The mixed problem cuts both ways. Helpers are needed and disappointed, but satisfying them without limit can create a larger injured group among new subjects.

reviewCards.front: A city opens its gates to a new ruler, then complains two days later. Which two groups should you identify?
reviewCards.back: Identify the locals injured by entry and the helpers disappointed by their reward. A mixed principality creates both pressures at once.

reviewCards.front: A ruler governs a different-language province from the capital. Why is that dangerous?
reviewCards.back: Distance hides disorders until they are large. Residence or a close local seat lets the ruler see early trouble and restrain officials before resentment hardens.

reviewCards.front: Why can a colony be less dangerous than a moving garrison?
reviewCards.back: A colony injures fewer people and anchors rule in key places, while a garrison spreads cost and hardship through the whole state. The injury still must be faced honestly.

reviewCards.front: A weak local chief asks for more boats and territory. What is the mixed-principality caution?
reviewCards.back: Protect minor powers without enlarging them. They help balance the region only while they remain useful and unable to become the next major threat.

reviewCards.front: A council invites a distant kingdom to avoid a present war. What question should follow?
reviewCards.back: Ask whether the invitation only defers war to the outsider's advantage and gives malcontents a stronger patron inside the region.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Treat annexation as a live transition, not a completed event. Map the groups injured by entry, the helpers who expect rewards, the local rules that should not be disturbed, and the outside powers that could turn resentment into a regional threat.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a territory has just been added to an older state, then list injured locals and disappointed helpers before judging whether the new ruler is secure.
If the acquired place differs in language, customs, or laws, then prefer residence or a close local seat so disorders are seen before they grow.
If the choice is roaming force or small local anchors, then compare how many people each injures and whether the plan creates a place to hear grievances early.
If someone proposes inviting a stronger outside power to avoid present conflict, then ask which malcontents will gain a patron and whether the war is only being deferred.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Choose one current annexation, takeover, or occupation story. Write four lines: injured locals, disappointed helpers, local rules not to touch yet, and the foreign power that could become a shelter.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once this week, read a political story about a newly controlled place and mark whether the ruler is using residence, colonies, garrisons, minor powers, or foreign allies.

memorableLines.text: Victory is the start of the transition, not the end of the problem.
memorableLines.why: It stops the reader from treating conquest as completion.

memorableLines.text: A distant ruler hears about disorders only after they have become organized.
memorableLines.why: It captures why residence matters in one concrete warning.

memorableLines.text: Do not commit a blunder to avoid a war that delay will hand to someone else.
memorableLines.why: It preserves the deferred-war lesson without flattening it into pacifism or aggression.

chapters.title: Why the Kingdom of Darius, Conquered by Alexander, Did Not Rebel Against the Successors of Alexander at His Death
chapters.hook: A minister can hand you a palace key and still bring no province behind him.
chapters.counterintuition: Retention belongs to the conquered state's shape. Servants who served at a prince's pleasure fall with him; barons who keep their own followers survive the conquest and instead become the entry points for revolt.
chapters.tryThisNow: Choose one institution from public reporting. Mark removable servants and actors with their own followers, assets, or inherited authority, then name the entry danger and the holding danger.
chapters.keyTakeaway: A conquest is hard or easy to hold according to the subject state's structure: removable servants make entry harder and retention easier, while rooted barons reverse the risk.

breakdown.fastRead: A palace aide defects with stamped orders in his sleeve, but no village flag moves with him. Across the border, one angry baron can open roads, grain stores, and towers because people know his house. Those are different states. In one, power runs through servants who depend on the prince. In the other, power lives in local lords with their own subjects. Do not ask first how brilliant the winner is. Ask whether people obey court servants or rooted powers that can survive the ruling family.
breakdown.deepRead:
A palace minister can promise a gate and still bring no country. If his office exists only by the prince's favor, then his defection may be useful for intrigue but weak for conquest. The people do not follow him because they do not love him as a lord. A kingdom run from one center through servants gives an outsider few independent centers of discontent to invite in.

Picture a wall map under a desk lamp, with minister photos on one side and provincial flags on the other. The photos look important until no roads, granaries, or radio towers move with them. The provincial flags matter more when each flag belongs to a local house that people obey by old attachment. Those houses can unlock entry before conquest and then make holding dangerous after conquest.

Darius's empire looked more like the first structure. Once Alexander defeated Darius in the field and the prince's line was gone, the servants who remained had little credit with the people. The difficulty was entry. The holding problem was smaller because no baronial layer survived with its own loved subjects.

France shows the opposite logic. A malcontent baron can help an invader enter. But the same kind of lord remains after victory, still rooted, still honored, still able to become the head of a fresh movement. The limit is simple: centralized rule is not always better, and local lords are not always worse. The point is diagnostic. Entry and retention reverse depending on where real authority lives.
breakdown.fullRead:
Stand in the war tent before the first bribe is paid. Some kingdoms are ruled by one prince through servants. These servants may be called ministers, governors, or administrators, but their authority comes from the ruler's favor and can be shifted at will. Other kingdoms are ruled by a prince among barons, and those barons hold rank by antiquity of blood, land, and local recognition. Their subjects know them as lords and feel a natural attachment to them.

The first structure is hard to enter. You cannot easily be called in by local princes because there are none with independent authority. You may corrupt a minister, but he cannot carry the people with him. The state is more united against an outside attack, so the invader must rely more on his own strength and less on revolt inside the kingdom. That is the hard part.

After victory, the same structure becomes easier to hold. If the ruling family is removed and the army is beaten in the field, the remaining servants have little standing of their own. They were not trusted as independent lords before conquest, so they are less dangerous after it. They can be replaced, absorbed, or ignored in a way rooted barons cannot. This is why the kingdom of Darius did not rise against Alexander's successors in the way a baronial realm might have. The answer is not a tribute to Alexander's charm. It is a reading of Darius's government.

A frontier kingdom with hereditary barons reverses the pattern. Entry may be easier because malcontents always exist, and a baron with roads, granaries, soldiers, and local affection can open the way. He can make victory easier. But he also remains a problem when the battle ends. If you cannot satisfy him, he can complain with authority. If you crush him, other local houses learn what your rule means. If you leave him in place, he may lead the next movement. Removing the family of the prince is not enough, because the lords that remain can become new heads of resistance.

A fair objection is that the servant-ruled state sounds stronger in every way. It is not. It may be brittle at the top. If the central army and ruling family fall, there may be no rooted layer able to organize national resistance. A baronial state, by contrast, may be messy before conquest and stubborn after it. The useful comparison is not strong versus weak. It is hard-entry/easier-holding versus easier-entry/hard-holding.

The examples named in the source make the contrast plain. The Turk rules through servants who are shifted and changed at will. France contains ancient lords with prerogatives the king cannot remove without peril. Darius's empire is read through the first pattern. Spain, France, and Greece gave the Romans repeated trouble because many local principalities and memories remained for a time. Once those memories faded under long Roman rule, possession grew more secure.

Use this as a test whenever someone explains conquest by the conqueror alone. Ask what remained after the field victory. Were there servants whose credit died with the prince, or barons whose authority lived in land, name, and local affection? Did the invader need to beat a united center, or could he enter through a malcontent?
